newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: U.S. says enough forces to stop Asia conflicts.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says enough forces to stop Asia conflicts.

text.p: The United States said on Tuesday it has sufficient forces in the Asia-Pacific region to handle any flare up in tension and to ensure rival countries settle disputes peacefully.

Rear Admiral Michael Haskins, commander of the U.S. Navy in Japan, told a defence conference in Singapore that one of the U.S. roles was to "deter the rise of any hegemonistic power or coalition" in the region.
He said disputes like the one over the South China Sea Spratly islands or overlapping economic zones at sea should not degenerate "from international discussion into actual physical dispute".
"We have forces forward deployed in the area to make sure the players resolve the dispute peacefully," Haskins said.
Washington could continue to be "a security guard to patrol the area and maintain the free flow" of trade in the region, he added.

There has been widespread concern in much of Asia over the depth of the U.S. commitment to the role of policeman in a region where an escalating arms race and competing claims to mineral resources could lead to trouble.

Sam Bateman, executive director of the Centre for Maritime Policy in Australia, told the conference that disputes over islands and potential mineral resources stretched from northeast to Southeast Asia.

The disputes range from that over the Spratlys, claimed in whole or in part by China, Vietnam, Taiwan, Malaysia, Brunei and the Philippines, to those between Japan, China and Taiwan over the Senkaku, or Diaoyu, island group in the East China Sea.
Shingo Nishimura, a conservative member of Japan's main opposition New Frontier Party, landed on one of the Senkakus on Tuesday, prompting an angry protest from China.
"Not only are marine resources an important dimension of Asia-Pacific security, but all the trends at present are in the wrong direction," Bateman said.
"The dual concerns of securing offshore zones and vital shipping are major factors in the acquisition of naval arms in the region," he added.
Bateman said only a handful of countries had settled competing claims over exclusive economic zones.
He said the current system of exploiting marine resources based on national rights and obligations was "ineffective" because countries were acting largely in their own interest.
"These problems will continue, with consequent risks to national security unless new approaches to resource exploitation are found," Bateman said.
